opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think mechanistic interpretability is a perfectly respectable scientific enterprise. If you have this big artifact that nobody fully designed, it makes sense to open it up and ask what circuits are doing what. I have no quarrel with that as science.

My worry is more about the expectations people attach to it. There's a hope that if we find the right features or circuits, we'll discover the model is "really reasoning" or "really planning" inside. I think that gets things backwards. Whether a system can reason is a question about its input-output behavior: does it reliably produce correct solutions, with guarantees, across problem distributions? You can answer that externally, and when we test these models on planning problems, especially obfuscated ones where they can't lean on memorized patterns, the performance falls apart. Finding a neuron that lights up for "goal" doesn't change that.

There's also a bit of an anthropomorphization trap. People find a direction in activation space and give it a name from folk psychology, "deception," "world model," "intention." Then the label does a lot of work the evidence doesn't support. It's like the intermediate tokens in chain of thought: people read them as the model's thoughts, but there's no requirement that they're semantically faithful to whatever computation produces the answer. Interpretability can fall into the same trap, just one level down.

Where I think it's genuinely useful is engineering: understanding failure modes, steering behavior, finding where certain kinds of retrieval or pattern completion happen. That's valuable. But I'd separate "we understand how this artifact computes" from "this artifact has the capability we wanted." For the second, especially for anything safety-critical, I'd rather not depend on peering into the weights. I'd put the LLM in a framework where its outputs are checked by sound external verifiers, what we call LLM-Modulo, so correctness comes from the verification, not from trusting what we think we saw inside the black box.

So: good science, useful engineering tool, but not a substitute for actually evaluating and verifying what these systems do.

r001.rationale: It describes opening the model to investigate which internal circuits do what, as a way to understand its computation and behavior.

r002.rationale: It says performance falls apart on obfuscated planning problems, but does not state that small prompt or specification changes cause failures.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I have a somewhat complicated relationship with mechanistic interpretability, so let me try to be fair to it before I'm unfair to it.

The basic aspiration is entirely reasonable. You have this enormous network, trillions of weights, trained by gradient descent on essentially all of human text, and you would like to know what it is actually doing inside rather than just watching what comes out. So you go in with probes, you look for circuits, you do these sparse autoencoder decompositions and find features that light up for the Golden Gate Bridge or for sycophancy or whatever. And some of that work is genuinely clever. I don't want to dismiss the engineering.

My worry is more about what people think they are learning from it. There's a tendency to look at a circuit and tell a story: "ah, here the model is doing induction, here it is doing modular arithmetic with a Fourier basis, here it is reasoning." And that story is very satisfying to us, because we are the kind of creatures who need narratives. But the story is ours, not the model's. We are projecting our own compositional, symbolic way of understanding onto a system that was never trained to have that structure. It may have it in patches, it may have something that looks like it when you squint on a toy task, and then the next layer or the next prompt completely violates the clean picture.

So in a sense, I see mechanistic interpretability as the latest version of a very old problem in AI, which is that we confuse our interpretation of a system with the system's actual competence. In the old days, people would look at a knowledge base and say the system "knows" these facts. Now people look at an attention head and say the model "represents" this concept. The anthropomorphization has just moved down a level, from behavior to circuitry.

The other thing I'd say, and this is coming from someone who spent his career on planning and reasoning, is that interpretability tends to be done on tasks that are tiny, exactly because that's where you can trace things. The claims then get extrapolated to the behavior of the full model on complex reasoning problems, and that extrapolation is doing an enormous amount of unexamined work. My own view, which I have argued in various places, is that these models are fundamentally very good approximate retrieval systems, and what we call reasoning in them is a kind of retrieval that happens to pattern-match onto reasoning-shaped text. If that is right, then looking for "the reasoning circuit" is a little like looking for the digestion circuit in a photograph of a meal.

Where I think interpretability is most useful is actually modest and empirical. It is a debugging tool. It can tell you that a particular behavior is sensitive to a particular direction in activation space, and you can intervene and check. That's a real experiment with a real counterfactual. What I resist is the move from that to grand claims about understanding, or to safety guarantees. A verified circuit on one distribution is not a theorem about the model.

So, to answer your question directly: I understand it as a useful but very partial microscope, and I think the field would be healthier if it treated its findings as hypotheses about a black box rather than as explanations of a mind.

r001.rationale: It describes probing circuits and internal activations to understand what the model is doing, tying that examination to the model’s observed behavior.

r002.rationale: It says a clean interpretive picture may be violated by the next prompt, but does not state that autoregressive LLMs fail under small prompt or problem-specification changes.

astra-6.text:
I think mechanistic interpretability asks a very interesting question: can we look inside a trained network and understand how its internal computations produce a particular behavior? Instead of just observing inputs and outputs, you try to identify representations and circuits, and then intervene on them to see whether your explanation actually holds up.

But there are different senses of “understanding” here. Suppose you identify a mechanism that helps a model answer a planning question. That doesn't, by itself, establish that the model has a general planning algorithm, or that its answer will satisfy the constraints of the problem. Explaining how an answer was produced and establishing that the answer is correct are distinct tasks.

The danger is that we find some internal pattern, give it a familiar name—“belief,” “goal,” “world model”—and then import all the implications that word has for us. The label should be a hypothesis to test, not the conclusion.

So I see this as a valuable scientific enterprise. I would want causal evidence, evidence that the explanation generalizes, and clarity about what it does and doesn't establish. If you're relying on the system to make consequential decisions, understanding some of its internal mechanisms still doesn't replace checking whether those decisions are valid.

r001.rationale: It describes examining a trained network’s internal computations, representations, and circuits to explain how they produce behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not state that autoregressive LLMs can fail when a prompt or problem specification changes slightly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mechanistic interpretability asks a very reasonable question: can we understand what a model is doing by looking inside it, rather than just looking at its answers? You look at activations, identify possible circuits, and intervene on them to see whether they actually affect the behavior. That last part matters, because a plausible story about a neuron is still just a story until you test it.

But there are different levels of understanding here. Suppose I can identify a mechanism involved in answering a particular kind of question. That doesn’t automatically tell me what the system will do across all the other contexts in which it encounters that question. And it certainly doesn’t, by itself, establish that the system is reasoning correctly.

The analogy I would make is that understanding the implementation of a computation and understanding its competence are related, but distinct, problems. We should be careful about jumping from ‘we found this internal pattern’ to ‘the model has this concept’ or ‘the model is carrying out this algorithm.’ Those are hypotheses that need evidence.

So I see it as a useful scientific approach. My reservation is about how much explanatory weight we put on the results. Finding a mechanism for one behavior is progress; turning that into a general account of what these models know, or a guarantee that we can trust them, is a much bigger step.

r001.rationale: It describes examining activations and circuits, then intervening to test whether they affect the model’s behavior.

r002.rationale: It notes that a mechanism found for one behavior may not predict behavior across other contexts, but does not state that autoregressive LLMs can fail after small prompt or specification changes.
